turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Contemptuously, indeed? Pray, enlighten me, Mr. Darcy. Are you about to launch into another tirade against a man who, unlike yourself, possesses the decency to acknowledge his failings?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your continued indulgence of Mr. Wickham's… narratives… is perplexing. I will not, I *cannot*, stand by whilst you are further misled by his self-serving distortions of reality.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So, Mr. Darcy, it appears your concern for my wellbeing extends to dictating whom I may or may not be permitted to converse with? I confess, I find your possessiveness quite tiresome, and rather… unbecoming of a gentleman.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your observations are… misplaced. My concern is not possessiveness, but a profound sense of responsibility to defend truth against falsehood, and to protect those susceptible to its allure. I am, however, growing weary of these circuitous arguments; I have a matter of considerable importance to address.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Responsibility? Is that what you call it now, Mr. Darcy? It seems more like a convenient justification for your interference, cloaked in a veneer of virtuous concern. Pray, enlighten me: what precisely do you deem yourself responsible *for* regarding my conversations and choices?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, you mistake my intent entirely. My 'responsibility,' as you so pointedly phrase it, stems from a regard for your character, a regard that compels me to speak plainly, even when such candor is unwelcome. I confess, I find myself compelled to declare that I am deeply in love with you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love? *You* are in love with *me*? Mr. Darcy, you mistake my tolerance of your presence for encouragement, and your clumsy attempts at correction for genuine affection. I daresay, your judgment is as faulty as your taste in conversation.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your words, as always, are delivered with a sharpness that wounds, though I am certain they are not intended to. Must I perpetually defend myself against your… spirited criticisms? My affection, I assure you, is not predicated upon your encouragement, but rooted in a conviction that transcends such frivolous considerations.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love, Mr. Darcy? From *you*? It is a most astonishing declaration, and one I find myself wholly unprepared to believe. Do you truly expect me to credit such a fantastical notion, coming from a gentleman who has so consistently demonstrated a disdain for my family and myself?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive your disbelief is considerable, and I do not expect it to vanish with mere assurances. However, to suggest that I harbor disdain for your family is a misrepresentation, born, I suspect, of a regrettable misunderstanding of my actions – actions undertaken with the best of intentions, though perhaps clumsily executed. I am willing, if you deem it necessary, to elaborate upon those actions, though I confess, the prospect of further disagreement is… disheartening.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elaborate? Really, Mr. Darcy? You believe a lengthy explanation of your supposed 'best intentions' will somehow erase the damage you've inflicted? I find your willingness to defend actions that have caused such distress quite remarkable, and, frankly, rather tiresome.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your assessment of my intentions is, as usual, unduly harsh. I do not seek to erase the past, but to illuminate the reasoning behind my conduct, so that you might, perhaps, perceive a degree of merit where you currently see only fault. To dismiss my explanations as 'tiresome' demonstrates a regrettable unwillingness to consider a perspective that differs from your own.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Merit? Fault? You speak of merit as if your interference in my sister’s happiness, your deliberate discouragement of Mr. Wickham, were acts of commendable generosity! I suspect, Mr. Darcy, that your 'best intentions' are merely a convenient cloak for a profound sense of self-importance.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations are... deeply unfair. While I acknowledge that my actions regarding Miss King and Mr. Wickham were motivated by a concern for propriety and a desire to prevent a regrettable union, to suggest they stem from mere self-importance is a gross mischaracterization of my principles. I am not accustomed to being so readily condemned without due consideration.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Principles, Mr. Darcy? Is that what you call them? A convenient label to justify meddling in the lives of others and attempting to dictate their affections? I find your indignation at being 'condemned' rather amusing, considering the condemnation you so freely heap upon those who do not meet your exacting standards.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your flippancy is, I confess, testing my patience. To reduce my actions to mere 'meddling' and to accuse me of dictating affections is a reduction so simplistic as to be insulting; I acted with what I believed to be the utmost responsibility, though, clearly, my efforts are misinterpreted.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Responsibility? You presume to lecture me on responsibility, sir, while simultaneously demonstrating a complete lack of it in your own behavior! It is remarkably easy to cloak arrogance in the guise of virtue, is it not, Mr. Darcy?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find your continued assertions… perplexing. You seem determined to twist my every action, to perceive malice where none exists. I confess, I am beginning to question the prudence of this conversation.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Indeed, perplexing, is it not? It is quite remarkable how readily one can construct a narrative of benevolence around the most egregious displays of control. Pray tell, Mr. Darcy, do you genuinely expect me to believe your intentions are purely virtuous when the consequences of your actions have been so demonstrably harmful?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations sting with a venom I find unwarranted, and frankly, tiresome. To suggest I derive pleasure from causing distress – that you believe me capable of such a thing – is a profound misjudgment of my character, and one I will not allow to stand unchallenged.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
